cells.tense: You are here at the threshold, meeting what arrives, and it does not throw you. Something finishes because it is finished — you honor that and open your hands to what comes next. Nothing dramatic, nothing delayed. Reading what is entering is simply something you can do, and you do it without flinching.
cells.ask: Set fair terms with the person beside you for something new — a share, a swap, a turn — and say the terms out loud.
cells.core: You know how endings work. You arrive at the door of something new without pushing at it, and you let a thing be finished when it is finished. Both the end and the next thing can sit in your hands at once, and that is what keeps you steady through a change. That same steadiness is what fairness is made of — you can feel what is right without grinding through the math. You read what is arriving and you move toward it evenly. What this ease can carry you into next is a real exchange with someone, one where you give something and let something come back, without keeping score.
cells.sheetLine: You meet what arrives, and you let what is finished end.
cells.verb: letting what is finished end, and meeting what arrives next
cells.place: the threshold where what is coming in first makes contact

cells.tense: You are already living past this moment, ending things before they have had a chance to live. You call it clearing space. You are bracing — and the movement you call liberation is the movement of someone who cannot stay still. The upheaval keeps coming, and you keep calling it freedom.
cells.ask: Stay with one thing long enough to hear how the other person feels about it before you finish it, and keep their feeling theirs.
cells.core: You can meet what arrives. When a close person tells you something hard, you can feel it with them and stay yourself, which is rarer than it sounds — most people either go cold or disappear into the other person's weather. That is the capacity you already have. In its place right now, you get ahead of the moment: a new thing shows up and before it has had a chance to be anything, you are sweeping it out, and the ending feels like liberation. It is not destruction, but it is fear wearing the wrong word. What is missing is not courage. It is the other person in the room — the specific weight of what they feel about the thing you are about to end, felt as theirs and not converted into yours. The next ending is still available once you actually know what you are ending.
cells.sheetLine: You are ending things before they get a chance to live.
cells.verb: letting what is finished end, and meeting what arrives next
cells.place: the threshold where what is coming in first makes contact

cells.tense: You are standing at a door that is already behind you, holding on to something that has finished. What is entering now cannot reach you, because you are still turned toward what is gone. The arriving thing is kept at arm's length by loyalty to the finished one.
cells.ask: Let one unfinished feeling pull you forward — say yes to the next small thing you actually want, and let it move you.
cells.core: You know how to want something and walk toward it. When a genuine feeling is under your feet — not a plan, a feeling — it turns into direction on its own, and you keep that direction through resistance without burning out. That is real, and it is yours. Here it is starved: the next thing is at the threshold waiting to be met, and you are still holding what ended. You call it loyalty. Standing at the closed door takes the energy that would move you, so the doorway stays empty. You do not have to let go of what came before to let the next thing reach you. One small movement toward what you actually want is enough to start the pull, and the wanting is the direction. The way back is taken today, in the size of one yes, or it is not taken at all — last week's choosing cannot be changed and next week's cannot be pre-signed.
cells.sheetLine: Holding what is finished is keeping what is arriving out.
cells.verb: letting what is finished end, and meeting what arrives next
cells.place: the threshold where what is coming in first makes contact

cells.tense: Something is already ending, and you are writing next year's plan as if it were still alive. You talk about the arrangement as a permanent fact. What you are doing is managing something that is over, and calling it the present. The ending is happening through your hands and going unnamed.
cells.ask: Give one thing that is fading a name — say out loud what it actually is now, and let the naming stand.
cells.core: You can give a shape to things. When something is tangled, you can organize it into a form that other people can walk through — a clear container, a reliable structure — and in your presence things make sense. That is the capacity here. Right now you are running the next version of something while its ending goes unnamed. You carry an arrangement — a role, a routine, a way things get done — as if it were still true, and steer what comes next through your hands, without saying that you are doing either. The ending is not happening to you. It is already yours to make, and you have not said so. A plain sentence about what is over is the smallest first move, and the room gets calmer once the sentence is out.
cells.sheetLine: Something is ending in your hands and you haven't said so.

cells.place: the threshold where what is coming in first makes contact
